title: Spotify as a case study in making something people want
summary: Garry Tan uses the New Yorker's Spotify profile to show the anatomy of making something people want: a precisely defined broken problem, a measurable product bar (200 ms), proprietary tech that only needs to buy a 6-month head start, and a painful schlep that becomes the moat.

principles.text: Start with a simple problem statement: know exactly what is broken. Era-defining startups begin this way.
principles.quote: They started with a simple problem statement. All of the great era-defining startups seem to start that way. What was broken? They knew exactly what was broken.

principles.text: Define a concrete, measurable success bar for the product so you know what winning looks like.
principles.quote: They knew how to measure success. Clearly if you could make a streaming service act as if it were on your local hard drive, you could win.

principles.text: Your technical advantage doesn't need to last forever; it only needs to keep copycats a step behind while you pull ahead.
principles.quote: You don't need a technological advantage that lasts forever (though of course that'd be preferable) — just one that will last enough such that your competitors can only copy your innovation from 6 months ago.

principles.text: Doing something that hadn't been done before is a real edge, even though software can be cloned.
principles.quote: Novel tech is not an infinite defense, but it was enough of one for Spotify to get off the ground.

principles.text: The schlep is the moat: hard, grinding work founders would avoid if they knew it upfront creates protectable long-term value.
principles.quote: If founders knew how much work these things would be, often they wouldn't do it. But they do, and that's protectable long term enterprise value.

principles.text: Beat the incumbent behavior (piracy) by building a better product, because people just want a great experience.
principles.quote: What if you can make a better product than piracy?
